rubric.why: A solution is defined as a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture containing solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for homogeneous mixture and 1 mark for identifying solute and solvent as its components.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
The substance present in the larger amount is usually the solvent, and the substance dissolved in it is the solute.

items.followUp: State two differences between a true solution and a colloid.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light (the Tyndall effect).
rubric.description: States that colloids scatter light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the Tyndall effect or light scattering.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stable, non-settling nature of colloids.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect.
Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.

items.followUp: Why does the atomic radius increase down a group in the periodic table?

rubric.why: Down a group, additional electron shells make the outer electrons farther from the nucleus.
rubric.description: Explains that atomic size or distance of outer electrons increases down the group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increase in atomic size or distance of outer electrons.

rubric.why: The nucleus attracts the outer electrons less strongly, so metals lose them more readily and their reactivity increases.
rubric.description: Connects weaker attraction or easier electron loss with increased reactivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the weaker attraction/easier loss explanation and the resulting increase in reactivity.

modelAnswer: Down a group, atomic size increases and the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus.
The nucleus attracts these electrons less strongly, so they are lost more easily and the reactivity of metals increases.

items.followUp: What happens to the electropositivity of an element when its ionization energy increases?

rubric.why: Electropositivity and ionization energy vary inversely.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an inverse relationship.

rubric.why: An element with low ionization energy loses electrons more easily and is more electropositive.
rubric.description: Explains the relationship in terms of ease of electron removal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking low ionization energy with easy electron loss/high electropositivity.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
An element with low ionization energy loses electrons easily and is highly electropositive.

items.followUp: State three observations made in Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment and give one conclusion from them.

rubric.why: The majority of alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation that most particles passed undeflected.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were slightly deflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation of small-angle deflections.

rubric.why: A very small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles or bounced back.
rubric.description: States that very few alpha particles were strongly deflected or bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation of large deflections or backward scattering.

rubric.why: The passage of most alpha particles without deflection showed that most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.description: Concludes that most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this conclusion.

rubric.why: The rare large deflections showed that positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.
rubric.description: Concludes that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or bounced back.
The atom is mostly empty space.
Most of the atom’s positive charge and mass are concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.

items.followUp: Define a metallic bond and state two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the metallic bond as attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Metals generally have a lustrous appearance.
rubric.description: Gives lustre as a property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for lustrous or shiny.

rubric.why: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets.
rubric.description: Gives malleability as a property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for malleable.

rubric.why: Metals can be drawn into wires.
rubric.description: Gives ductility as a property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ductile.

rubric.why: Metals conduct heat and electricity well because of their mobile electrons.
rubric.description: States that metals conduct heat or electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for good electrical or thermal conductivity.

modelAnswer: A metallic bond is the force of attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalized electrons.
Metals are lustrous.
Metals are malleable: they can be hammered into sheets.
Metals are ductile: they can be drawn into wires.
Metals conduct heat and electricity well.

items.followUp: Which contains more molecules: 18 g of water or 18 g of sucrose? Show the calculation.

rubric.why: Nine grams of water is 0.5 mol, or approximately 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.
rubric.description: Calculates the amount or number of molecules in the water sample.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct water calculation.

rubric.why: Nine grams of sucrose is approximately 0.0263 mol, or 1.58 × 10²² molecules, so water contains more molecules.
rubric.description: Calculates the sucrose amount and identifies water as having more molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct comparison, with water identified as containing more molecules.

modelAnswer: Given: m(H₂O) = 0.009 kg; M(H₂O) = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹; m(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) = 0.009 kg; M(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) = 0.342 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m / M; number of molecules = n × Nₐ, where Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
For water: n = 0.009 kg / 0.018 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.50 mol.
Number of H₂O molecules = 0.50 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.
For sugar: n = 0.009 kg / 0.342 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.0263 mol.
Number of sugar molecules = 0.0263 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ ≈ 1.58 × 10²² molecules.
Therefore, 9 g of H₂O has more molecules.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a compound and a mixture.

rubric.why: Elements in a compound are chemically combined in a fixed ratio; mixture components may be present in variable proportions.
rubric.description: Differentiates compounds and mixtures by how their components combine or their composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-ratio compound versus variable-proportion mixture distinction.

rubric.why: A compound is separated into its elements by chemical methods, whereas mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Differentiates compounds and mixtures by the methods used to separate their components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chemical separation of compounds versus physical separation of mixtures.

modelAnswer: In a compound, elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio; in a mixture, substances may be present in any proportion.
The components of a compound can be separated by chemical methods, whereas the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
